steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
A transformer is a sequence-to-sequence neural network that relies almost entirely on a single idea—attention—to model relationships inside a sequence, instead of the recurrence or convolution used in earlier architectures. Conceptually you can think of it as a stack of identical “reasoning layers,” each of which performs three main steps:

1. Look at every token in the sequence and ask, “Which other tokens should I pay attention to when representing this one?”  
2. Gather information from those tokens in parallel, producing a richer representation for each position.  
3. Pass each position-wise representation through a small feed-forward network to let the model transform or re-mix the gathered information before sending it to the next layer.

Below are the key ideas, stated informally.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Tokens, embeddings, and positions
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Any input (words, sub-words, characters, image patches, etc.) is first mapped to a vector—that’s its embedding.  
• Because a transformer has no notion of “left” or “right” built in, we add or concatenate a position code to each embedding so the model can tell the first token from the fifth, and so on.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Self-attention: asking and answering “Who matters to me?”
----------------------------------------------------------------
For every token position i we create three learned vectors:

    Query  (Qᵢ)   – what i is looking for  
    Key    (Kⱼ)   – what each other position j offers  
    Value  (Vⱼ)   – the actual information j can supply  

Attention weight between i and j = similarity(Qᵢ, Kⱼ) → softmax.  
Then we blend (sum) all Vⱼ, weighted by those scores, to form a new vector Zᵢ for position i. Because every position attends to every other, the layer can model arbitrary long-range dependencies in one step.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Multi-head attention: seeing relationships from many angles
----------------------------------------------------------------
Instead of doing that calculation once, we do it h times with different learned projections. Each “head” may notice different kinds of patterns (syntax, agreement, synonymy, etc.). We then concatenate the h results and project them back to the original dimensionality. Multi-head = “parallel attention specialists.”

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Add & Norm, Feed-Forward, and stacking
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Residual connection: The attention output is added to the original input so the layer can either keep or refine information (eases training).  
• Layer normalization: stabilizes the scale of activations.  
• Position-wise feed-forward network: a small MLP (same weights for every position) lets each token process its freshly gathered context.  
• We stack N identical blocks so that information can be refined iteratively.

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. Encoder, decoder, and masks (in the original “Transformer”)
----------------------------------------------------------------
Encoder = stack that ingests the source sequence and outputs contextualized vectors.  
Decoder = similar stack, but it has two attentions:
  – Masked self-attention (each target position can only look leftward so we don’t peek at future words).  
  – Encoder–decoder attention (each target position attends to the encoded source).  
During inference the decoder is run step-by-step, appending one generated token at a time.

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Training objective
----------------------------------------------------------------
For translation or language modeling, the model is trained to predict the next token (cross-entropy loss) given the ground-truth context, with teacher forcing, back-propagated through all layers.

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Why is this powerful?
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Parallelizable: Attention over an entire sequence can be computed in one matrix multiplication, allowing GPU/TPU speedups.  
• Long-range modeling: Any token can interact with any other in one hop.  
• Scalability: Simply increasing layers, width, or heads (plus data) keeps improving performance.  
• Generality: The same building block works for text, vision, audio, protein sequences, etc.

----------------------------------------------------------------
8. Limitations (conceptual)
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Quadratic cost in sequence length (attention matrix).  
• No built-in recurrence; position information must be engineered.  
• Needs large data & compute to reach full potential.

In essence, a transformer layer is a content-aware “mixing board” that lets every token rewrite itself as a weighted combination of all others, repeated multiple times to progressively refine representations. That simple idea, executed in parallel and at scale, is what powers most state-of-the-art language and vision models today.
